title: KV shadowing and op-offload exploration
content:
Summary

This note captures a set of small, targeted experiments we ran to understand the tradeoffs of shadowing KV-cache state while opportunistically offloading compute-heavy ops between Triton, TensorRT (TRT), and our custom CUDA kernels. The goal: identify low-effort runtime heuristics that reduce tail latency regressions when we switch kernels or fallback between runtimes, while preserving burst throughput and KV cache hit quality.

Why this matters (short):
- Model serving latency is sensitive to small changes in where attention/softmax/gelu kernels run.
- A kernel switch can invalidate assumptions about KV-format, alignment, and hidden-dtype, causing micro-regressions that cascade into tail spikes.
- We want graceful fallbacks with minimal artifacts (no model re-serialize) and minimal cache churn.

Key ideas explored:
1) KV-shadowing: maintain a parallel, lightweight shadow cache in the runtime that mirrors the primary KV cache but stores pointers/headers for alternate kernel formats. Shadow entries are populated lazily.
2) Op-offload windows: allow a request to be routed to an alternate kernel only if a confidence window (based on recent successful calls) is satisfied; otherwise force execution on the primary runtime.
3) Format-compatibility probes: tiny microkernels that run on a subset of layers to check compatibility and warm up alternate runtimes without full execution.
4) Eviction policy awareness: integrate shadowed entries into eviction heuristics to avoid thrashing when kernels flip back and forth.

Experimental setup (hardware / software):
- HW: 2x A100 nodes (primary TRT node with 80GB), 2x RTX6000 (custom-kernel node), 1x CPU host for Triton orchestration.
- SW: TRT 8.6, Triton 23.10, CUDA 12.2, custom kernels built with nvcc 12.2 + cuBLAS/cuDNN, runtime branch kv-shadowing-explore (proto).
- Models: Llama-2-13B quantized FP16, and a distilled 6B variant used to test sequence-length sensitivity.
- Workloads: Mix of short-chat bursts (seq_len 32, high QPS), and long-context streams (seq_len 1024, low QPS).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, token-per-second, KV cache hit ratio (logical), shadow population latency, memory delta, frequency of format-conversion ops.

Experiments and observations:

A) Lazy shadow population (baseline):
- Implementation: On first fallback to TRT for a request with existing primary KV entries, we create shadow headers only (meta describing keys: shape, dtype, contiguous flag) without copying tensors. Full shadow tensor materialized on second access.
- Observation: Shadow headers cost negligible memory and let the scheduler quickly decide if TRT can be used for a particular request. Materialization-on-demand causes occasional 1-5 ms stalls on first deep fallback for long-context requests.
- Tradeoff: lowers steady-state overhead, but increases cold-fallback latency.

B) Probe microkernel + warmup window:
- Implementation: For a candidate runtime switch, run a 2-layer forward with the target runtime on the same KV prefix (cheap microkernel). If outputs match within tolerance, mark runtime "warmed" for that prefix for N secs.
- Observation: Warmup reduced p99 spikes by ~12% for mixed workloads. Probe cost ~0.4ms per attempt and usually amortized over subsequent tokens. However, for very short interactions (1-2 tokens) probe increases end-to-end latency.

C) Eviction-aware shadow TTLs:
- Implementation: If a KV entry in primary is marked as hot, we set a longer TTL for its shadow counterpart; evicted shadows are deprioritized before primary entries.
- Observation: Prevented thrashing in scenarios where routing oscillated between TRT and custom-kernel nodes due to autoscaling-induced capacity changes. Memory overhead ~6% on average.

D) Format conversion by pointer rewrite (no-copy) vs copy-on-convert:
- Pointer-rewrite approach: maintain multiple views with different strides/offsets referencing same underlying allocation. Conversion is O(1) if layout-compatible; else fallback to copy.
- Copy approach: eagerly copy into target layout on first materialization.
- Observation: Pointer-rewrite saved 8-20% latency in best cases but required stricter alignment invariants and more complex allocator bookkeeping. Copy-on-convert simpler but produced spikes on high sequence-length fallbacks.

E) Scheduling heuristic: recent-success ratio + token-budget
- Heuristic: route to alternate runtime if (recent_successes / recent_attempts) > 0.8 AND current token budget (as measured by kv-cache availability and batch headroom) > threshold. Otherwise prefer primary.
- Observation: Simple rule-of-thumb gave most of the benefit; complicated ML-based routing models did not materially outperform this baseline in our experiments.

Failures and surprising behaviours:
- TRT custom fusion on certain attention variants produced numerically different KV keys (tiny fp16 rounding) that made equality-based cache lookups fail. We added a tolerant lookup mode that hashes with epsilon.
- When multiple fallbacks happened concurrently for the same user session, the shadow population rate caused transient OOMs due to duplicate materialization attempts. We mitigated with per-session shadow in-flight dedupe.

Recommended short-term changes (practical):
1) Implement lazy shadow headers + on-demand materialization as default (low risk).
2) Add probe microkernel hooks but gate them by request length (disable for requests <= 4 tokens).
3) Add a tolerant-hash lookup mode (epsilon-based) when switching runtimes to avoid exact-equality misses.
4) Keep pointer-rewrite allocator as an opt-in flag for stable model shapes; otherwise use copy-on-convert.
5) Add per-session dedupe token to prevent parallel materialization races.

Questions / open items:
- What tolerance thresholds for probe acceptance are safe across models? We need a small sweep across 4 models and perturbation magnitudes.
- How should shadow TTL interact with Dedicated vs Hosted routing policies (tenant isolation constraints)?
- Can we expose a developer toggle to pin a model to always use a single runtime to avoid fallback churn for critical customers?

Quick checklist for next lab iteration:
- [ ] Run numeric-tolerance sweep on 2x 13B and 7B models (range: 1e-3 to 1e-6)
- [ ] Implement in-flight dedupe for shadow population (mutex per session key)
- [ ] Add coarse telemetry events: shadow_hit, shadow_materialize_ms, probe_success
- [ ] Add e2e canary test that flips runtime for 1% of traffic for 24h and compares p99 and token-rate

Appendix: reproduction notes (commands)
- micro-bench probe: ./bench/probe --model llama-13b --pages 2 --target trt --seq 128 --repeat 500
- shadow stress: ./bench/shadow_stress --qps 400 --seq 512 --sessions 2000 --enable-pointer-rewrite

Closing notes:
The experiments show that a combination of lazy shadowing, small probe warmups, and simple recent-success routing yields the best risk/benefit profile for incremental rollout of TRT/custom-kernel fallbacks. Most customer-impacting regressions came from exact-match KV lookups and duplicate materializations; both are solvable without heavy infra changes.

If folks on infra/routing agree, I propose we land a conservative default: lazy headers + probe microkernel (disabled for very short requests) + per-session dedupe, then run a two-week canary on a small traffic slice.

Comments welcome — especially from Mateo (allocator edgecases) and Chen (probe kernel stability).
